entry: Branch of mathematics that generalizes [[Arithmetic|arithmetic]] by using letters, called variables, to stand for numbers. Arithmetic operates only on specified numbers, whereas elementary algebra applies operations to numbers, variables and terms. By convention, multiplication signs are omitted (3 × x² is written 3x²), and terms with the highest power come first. Variables allow general relationships to be stated concisely and unknown quantities to be solved for; many relationships in science and mathematics are expressed as algebraic equations. Elementary algebra is typically taught in secondary school and introductory college courses in the United States. Unlike [[Abstract algebra|abstract algebra]], it is concerned only with real and complex numbers. Core topics include [[Linear equation|linear equations]], [[Polynomial|polynomials]] and [[Quadratic equation|quadratic equations]].

Fundamental physical constant equal to the magnitude of the electric charge on an electron. Its value is defined as exactly 1.602176634×10⁻¹⁹ C, and it is one of the seven defining constants of the [[International System of Units|International System of Units (SI)]]. Before the 2019 revision of the SI it was determined experimentally. Robert A. Millikan and Harvey Fletcher's [[Oil drop experiment|oil drop experiment]] first measured it directly, in 1909, within 0.6% of the modern value. All known elementary particles carry charges that are integer multiples of the charge on the [[Quark|down quark]], which is one-third of the elementary charge; down quarks cannot be isolated.

Subatomic particle that is not composed of other particles. The [[Standard Model|Standard Model]] of particle physics recognizes 17 distinct elementary particles: 12 [[Fermion|fermions]] and five [[Boson|bosons]]. Counting flavor, color and antimatter variants, there are 61. Fermions, which include [[Lepton|leptons]] such as the [[Electron|electron]] and the quarks that make up protons and neutrons, have half-integer spin. Bosons, which carry forces, have integer spin. The Standard Model omits [[Gravity|gravity]], and some of its parameters are unexplained.

Extinct flightless bird of the order Aepyornithiformes, native to [[Madagascar|Madagascar]]. Elephant birds were [[Herbivore|herbivores]] and major components of the island's ecosystems before humans arrived. *Aepyornis maximus* was possibly the largest bird to have lived, and its eggs were the largest known from any amniote. The birds probably died out around 1000 AD, likely because of human activity. Their closest living relatives are the [[Kiwi (bird)|kiwi]] of [[New Zealand|New Zealand]], which suggests that flightlessness in these ratites evolved independently rather than through the breakup of [[Gondwana|Gondwana]].

Largest living land animal, a herbivorous mammal of the family Elephantidae. Three species are recognized: the [[African bush elephant|African bush elephant]], the African forest elephant and the [[Asian elephant|Asian elephant]]. They are the only surviving members of the order [[Proboscidea|Proboscidea]], whose extinct relatives include [[Mammoth|mammoths]] and [[Mastodon|mastodons]]. Features include a prehensile trunk, tusks derived from incisor teeth, and large ears that help regulate body temperature. Elephants live in sub-Saharan Africa and South and Southeast Asia, in habitats from [[Savanna|savannas]] to forests and marshes, and as keystone species they shape their environments. Females live in family groups led by a matriarch, while males leave at puberty. Elephants can live up to 70 years in the wild. The African bush and Asian elephants are listed as endangered and the African forest elephant as critically endangered, with the [[Ivory|ivory]] trade among the biggest threats.

Height of a geographic location above or below a fixed reference point, most commonly a reference [[Geoid|geoid]], a model of mean sea level. The term is used for points on the Earth's surface, while altitude describes points above it, such as aircraft, and depth describes points below it. Elevation differs from distance from the Earth's center: because of the equatorial bulge, [[Mount Everest|Mount Everest]] has the largest elevation, while Chimborazo has the largest distance from the center. Topographic maps show elevation with contour lines. In [[Geographic information system|geographic information systems]], digital elevation models represent terrain as grids of elevation values.

Machine that transports people or freight vertically between levels. Most elevators are powered by electric motors that drive traction cables and counterweights, though some use hydraulic fluid to raise a piston. Early devices were hoists worked by people, animals or water power; the Roman [[Colosseum|Colosseum]] had roughly 25 elevators for raising animals to the arena floor. A screw-drive elevator built by Ivan Kulibin was installed in the Winter Palace in 1793, a step that led toward modern passenger elevators. In 1857 the first commercial passenger elevator, equipped with Elisha Graves Otis's safety brake, was installed in a New York City department store. Elevators make [[Skyscraper|skyscrapers]] practical, and high-speed models are common in tall buildings.

Greek-American film and theater director, producer and screenwriter. Born in Constantinople to Cappadocian Greek parents, he moved to the United States as a child. In 1947 he co-founded the Actors Studio, where, with Robert Lewis and Cheryl Crawford, he introduced method acting under Lee Strasberg. His films often addressed social issues, beginning with *Gentleman's Agreement*, with [[Gregory Peck|Gregory Peck]], which dealt with [[Antisemitism|antisemitism]]. *Gentleman's Agreement* and *On the Waterfront* won him [[Academy Awards|Academy Awards]] for Best Director, and he directed [[Marlon Brando|Marlon Brando]] in *A Streetcar Named Desire* and *On the Waterfront*. In 1952 he testified as a "friendly witness" before the House Un-American Activities Committee and named former associates as past Communist Party members. Critics said his testimony damaged the careers of former colleagues; Kazan said he had taken "only the more tolerable of two alternatives."

Romanian-born American writer, professor and [[The Holocaust|Holocaust]] survivor. Born in Sighet, he was deported with his family to [[Auschwitz concentration camp|Auschwitz]] in 1944, at age 15. His mother and younger sister died there, and he and his father were moved to Buchenwald. His memoir *Night* describes his experiences in the camps. He wrote 57 books, mostly in French and English, and taught humanities at Boston University. As an activist he spoke on the Holocaust and against [[Apartheid|apartheid]] and [[Genocide|genocide]], including in Rwanda and Cambodia. He received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1986 and was a main figure in establishing the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum. He was an outspoken advocate for Israel and said that [[Jerusalem|Jerusalem]] "belongs to the Jewish people."

Prophet and miracle worker of the northern Kingdom of Israel. According to the Books of Kings in the [[Hebrew Bible|Hebrew Bible]], Elijah lived during the reign of King Ahab in the 9th century BC. In 1 Kings 18 he defended the worship of [[Yahweh|Yahweh]] against that of the Canaanite deity [[Baal|Baal]]. He is credited with miracles including resurrection and an ascent to heaven, and his disciple Elisha succeeded him. Scholars generally agree that a historical figure named Elijah existed, although the biblical accounts are considered more legendary than historically accurate. In [[Judaism|Judaism]], his name is invoked at the weekly Havdalah rite that ends Shabbat, and some Jewish interpretations expect him to return at the end of times. The New Testament identifies John the Baptist as the Elijah promised in Malachi. The [[Quran|Quran]] presents him as a prophet, and he is venerated as the patron saint of [[Bosnia and Herzegovina|Bosnia and Herzegovina]].

American religious leader who led the [[Nation of Islam|Nation of Islam]] from 1933 until his death. Under his leadership the movement grew from a small [[Detroit|Detroit]]-based group into a nationwide organization with tens of thousands of members during the [[Civil rights movement|civil rights movement]]. He promoted black nationalism and a theology teaching that white people were "devils" created by a black scientist named Yakub. He has been described as both a black nationalist and a black supremacist. His son Wallace Muhammad transformed the group into a mainstream Islamic movement, and [[Louis Farrakhan|Louis Farrakhan]] later revived the Nation of Islam.

Hungarian noblewoman and alleged [[Serial killer|serial killer]]. Wife of Count Ferenc Nádasdy and a member of the powerful House of Báthory, she and four servants were accused of torturing and killing hundreds of girls and women between 1590 and 1610. The servants were tried and executed; Báthory was confined to her castle at Csejte, in present-day [[Slovakia|Slovakia]], until her death. Some scholars cite testimony from more than 300 witnesses, while others argue that the charges were a politically motivated effort to destroy her family's influence. Later legends of vampirism, including the tale that she bathed in the blood of virgins, are considered unreliable by modern historians.

American writer and activist, a leader of the [[Women's rights|women's rights movement]] in the mid- to late 19th century. She was the main force behind the 1848 Seneca Falls Convention, the first convention devoted solely to women's rights, and primary author of its Declaration of Sentiments. In 1851 she began a decades-long partnership with [[Susan B. Anthony|Susan B. Anthony]]; together they campaigned against slavery during the [[American Civil War|American Civil War]]. They opposed the Fifteenth Amendment, which would extend suffrage to Black men only, and the dispute split the movement. Some of Stanton's remarks in it were racially condescending, and [[Frederick Douglass|Frederick Douglass]] reproached her for them. Stanton was the first president of the National Woman Suffrage Association and, after the split healed, of the National American Woman Suffrage Association. She also wrote *The Woman's Bible*, which argued that the Bible's attitude toward women reflected prejudice.

American businesswoman convicted of [[Fraud|fraud]] in connection with the health technology company Theranos. Holmes founded Theranos in 2003, claiming to have developed [[Blood test|blood tests]] that needed only a fingerprick of blood. In 2015 [[Forbes|Forbes]] named her the youngest and wealthiest self-made female billionaire on the basis of a $9 billion valuation of the company; the following year it revised her net worth to zero as fraud allegations surfaced. Her [[Trial|trial]] ended in January 2022 with a conviction for defrauding investors and an acquittal on charges of defrauding patients. She was sentenced to 11¼ years in prison and, with Ramesh Balwani, ordered to pay $452 million in restitution.

Queen of the United Kingdom and other Commonwealth realms (r. 1952–2022). She succeeded her father, [[George VI|George VI]], in February 1952 and was crowned in [[Westminster Abbey|Westminster Abbey]] in 1953. Her reign of 70 years and 214 days was the longest of any British monarch. As a constitutional monarch she reigned through the decolonization of Africa, the [[The Troubles|Troubles]] in Northern Ireland, and the United Kingdom's accession to and withdrawal from the European Communities. She was advised by more than 170 prime ministers and met five popes and fourteen U.S. presidents. She died aged 96 at Balmoral Castle and was succeeded by her eldest son, [[Charles III|Charles III]].

American actress in film, stage and television, whose career spanned five decades. She played the witch Samantha Stephens in the sitcom *Bewitched*, a role that earned her five Primetime Emmy Award nominations and four Golden Globe nominations. The daughter of actor Robert Montgomery, she won a Theater World Award for her Broadway debut in *Late Love*. After *Bewitched* ended in 1972, she starred in television films including *The Legend of Lizzie Borden* (1975), playing [[Lizzie Borden|Lizzie Borden]]. She was also active in political causes and charity work.

British and American film actress, one of the most popular stars of classical Hollywood in the 1950s. She began as a child actress and became the world's highest-paid movie star in the 1960s. She won [[Academy Awards|Academy Awards]] for *Butterfield 8* (1960) and *Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf?* (1966). Her best-known role was in *Cleopatra* (1963), and she married co-star [[Richard Burton|Richard Burton]] in 1964; they appeared together in 11 films. Her private life, including two marriages to Burton, drew intense media scrutiny. In the 1980s she became one of the first celebrities to take part in HIV/AIDS activism. She co-founded the American Foundation for AIDS Research in 1985 and the Elizabeth Taylor AIDS Foundation in 1991.

Empress of Russia (r. 1741–1762) and daughter of [[Peter the Great|Peter the Great]]. She seized the throne in 1741 with military support, displacing the infant Ivan VI, and declared her nephew, the future Peter III, her heir. She is notable for deciding not to [[Capital punishment|execute]] anyone during her reign and for numerous construction projects. [[Moscow State University|Moscow State University]] was founded in 1755 through the efforts of [[Mikhail Lomonosov|Mikhail Lomonosov]] and Ivan Shuvalov, with Elizabeth signing its founding decree. Russia fought the [[Seven Years' War|Seven Years' War]], in which Russian troops briefly occupied [[Berlin|Berlin]]. She was the last member of the [[House of Romanov|House of Romanov]] on the male line to reign over Russia.

Large deer (*Cervus canadensis*), the second-largest member of the [[Deer|deer]] family, also called wapiti. Native to North America and parts of Central and East Asia, elk graze on grasses and browse leaves, twigs and bark in open forests. Males grow large antlers that they shed each year, and during the mating season they spar with antlers and bugle to establish dominance. The word elk originally referred to the European [[Moose|moose]], which North American colonists transferred to this animal. Mitochondrial DNA studies, beginning in 1998, showed that elk are a distinct species from the [[Red deer|European red deer]]. Elk have been introduced to [[Argentina|Argentina]] and [[New Zealand|New Zealand]], where they may threaten native ecosystems. As game, elk meat is lean and higher in protein than beef or chicken.

American [[Jazz|jazz]] singer and songwriter, known for her purity of tone, diction and scat singing. She rose to national fame with the Chick Webb Orchestra, whose recording of the nursery rhyme "A-Tisket, A-Tasket" made her and Webb famous. After Webb died she took over the band, and in 1942 she began a solo career. With Verve Records she recorded influential interpretations of the Great American Songbook. Her partnerships with [[Louis Armstrong|Louis Armstrong]] and [[Duke Ellington|Duke Ellington]] produced songs including "Cheek to Cheek" and "Dream a Little Dream of Me." Her last public performance was in 1993. Her honors include the Presidential Medal of Freedom and multiple [[Grammy Awards|Grammy Awards]].

Australian model, businesswoman and actress. She appeared a record five times on the cover of the *Sports Illustrated* Swimsuit Issue, earning the nickname "The Body," coined by [[Time (magazine)|Time]] in 1989. She founded the lingerie line Elle Macpherson Intimates and the skin care line The Body. She hosted and was executive producer of *Britain & Ireland's Next Top Model* (2010–2013), had a recurring role on *Friends*, and hosted an episode of *Saturday Night Live*.

American actress known for portraying complex women in dramas. She won the Academy Award for Best Actress for *Alice Doesn't Live Here Anymore* (1974), directed by [[Martin Scorsese|Martin Scorsese]], and a Tony Award for *Same Time, Next Year* (1975). Her other Oscar-nominated roles include *The Exorcist* (1973). Burstyn is one of the few performers to achieve the "Triple Crown of Acting" and has won two Primetime Emmy Awards. Since 2000 she has been co-president of the Actors Studio.

American comedian, actress and television host. Her sitcom *Ellen* (1994–1998) ran through her public coming out as a lesbian in 1997, and her character became the first openly gay lead on an American network television show. She hosted *The Ellen DeGeneres Show* from 2003 to 2022, which earned her 33 Daytime Emmy Awards. She voiced Dory in *Finding Nemo* (2003). In 2021 she announced the end of her talk show, following a Warner Bros. investigation into allegations of bullying, racism and misconduct by senior producers.

Liberian economist and politician, 24th president of [[Liberia|Liberia]] (2006–2018). Born in [[Monrovia|Monrovia]], she was educated in the United States, including at [[Harvard University|Harvard University]], and is a Harvard-trained economist. She served as Liberia's deputy minister of finance in the 1970s and as minister of finance from 1979 to 1980. After Samuel Doe seized power in 1980, she fled to the United States. She was sentenced to ten years' imprisonment in 1985 for criticizing the military government, but was later released. She finished second in the 1997 presidential election. She was the first woman in Africa elected as a head of state, and in 2011 she won the Nobel Peace Prize for efforts to bring women into the peacekeeping process. In 2016 she became the first woman to chair the Economic Community of West African States.

Island in the [[Arctic Archipelago|Arctic Archipelago]], Nunavut, Canada (pop., 2021: 144). Canada's northernmost and third-largest island, and the tenth largest in the world, it is slightly smaller than [[Great Britain|Great Britain]]. It is considered part of the Queen Elizabeth Islands. The Arctic Cordillera covers much of the island, making it the most mountainous in the archipelago, and more than one-fifth of the island is protected as Quttinirpaaq National Park. Cape Columbia, Canada's northernmost point of land, lies on the island. Paleo-Eskimo hunters, who mostly hunted [[Muskox|muskoxen]], left archaeological sites across it.
